items.stem: State what is meant by the term "overproduction of offspring".
items.answer: The production of more offspring than the environment can support, leading to competition and a struggle for survival
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the production of more offspring than the environment can support, leading to competition and a struggle for survival. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain Endler’s experiments on guppies.
items.answer: Guppies in streams with many predators have fewer, smaller spots; in low-predation streams males are more colourful; Endler moved guppies between pools and set up artificial ponds; within a few generations spot number changed according to predation pressure; shows balance of natural and sexual selection.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Guppies in streams with many predators have fewer, smaller spots; in low-predation streams males are more colourful; Endler moved guppies between pools and set up artificial ponds; within a few generations spot number changed according to predation pressure; shows balance of natural and sexual selection. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why is antibiotic resistance in bacteria evidence of natural selection?
options: Antibiotics create resistance genes on demand.
Resistant variants survive antibiotic treatment and reproduce, so their frequency increases.
All bacteria become resistant at once.
items.answer: Resistant variants survive antibiotic treatment and reproduce, so their frequency increases.
items.markingKey: C. Selection.

items.stem: "Individual organisms evolve during their lifetime." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Populations evolve over generations as allele frequencies change; individuals do not.
items.markingKey: Populations evolve over generations as allele frequencies change; individuals do not. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: After a drought on Daphne Major, the mean beak depth of medium ground finches changed from 8.98 mm to 9.29 mm in the next generation. Calculate the percentage change and suggest a biological explanation for it.
items.answer: +3.5 %; only birds with deeper beaks could crack the large, hard seeds that remained, so they survived and passed on alleles for deep beaks.
items.markingKey: % change = (9.29 − 8.98)/8.98 × 100 (M1) = +3.5 % (A1). Explanation (R1): only birds with deeper beaks could crack the large, hard seeds that remained, so they survived and passed on alleles for deep beaks.

items.stem:
Guppies taken from one population were placed in artificial ponds with either no predators or many predators (pike cichlids). The mean number of coloured spots per male was recorded every five generations.

Generation | No predators | Many predators
0 | 9.7 | 9.2
5 | 10.1 | 8.9
10 | 11.5 | 8.0
15 | 12.9 | 7.9
20 | 13.4 | 7.4

(a) State the mean number of spots in the no-predator pond after 15 generations. [1]
(b) Calculate the percentage change in spot number over 20 generations in each pond. [2]
(c) Explain the change in the pond with many predators. [3]
(d) Explain the change in the pond with no predators. [2]
items.answer: (a) 12.9 (b) no predators +38.1 %; many predators -19.6 % (c) Brightly spotted males are more conspicuous and more likely to be eaten; less spotted males survive and reproduce; alleles for fewer spots increase. (d) Females prefer more colourful males (sexual selection); without predation there is no survival cost, so spot number increases.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 12.9 (A1). (b) [2] (13.4 − 9.7)/9.7 × 100 = +38.1 % (A1); (7.4 − 9.2)/9.2 × 100 = -19.6 % (A1). (c) [3] Predation of conspicuous males (A1); survival and reproduction (A1); allele frequency change (A1). (d) [2] Female choice (A1); no predation cost (A1).

items.stem: Explain how sexual selection can produce traits that appear disadvantageous.
items.answer: Female choice, male–male competition; honest signals; peacock tail; guppy spots; trade-off with predation; Endler’s experiments.
items.markingKey: Female choice, male–male competition; honest signals; peacock tail; guppy spots; trade-off with predation; Endler’s experiments.

items.stem: "Natural selection is the only mechanism of evolutionary change." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Natural selection is the main cause of adaptation, but other mechanisms such as drift also change allele frequencies.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains adaptation in many examples (finches, moths, antibiotic resistance). Arguments against: genetic drift and gene flow change allele frequencies randomly or by migration; mutation supplies variation; sexual selection is a distinct process. Supported judgement: Natural selection is the main cause of adaptation, but other mechanisms such as drift also change allele frequencies. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Differences between individuals that are caused by genes and can be passed on to offspring"?
items.answer: heritable variation
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of heritable variation.

items.stem: Why must variation be heritable for natural selection to cause evolution?
options: Only genetic traits are passed to offspring, so only they can increase in frequency.
items.answer: Only genetic traits are passed to offspring, so only they can increase in frequency.
items.markingKey: D. Inheritance needed.

items.stem: Distinguish between natural selection and sexual selection.
items.answer: Natural selection favours traits that increase survival and reproduction in the environment; sexual selection favours traits that increase success in obtaining mates, which may reduce survival.
items.markingKey: Natural selection favours traits that increase survival and reproduction in the environment; sexual selection favours traits that increase success in obtaining mates, which may reduce survival. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which peppered moths in industrial Britain shows natural selection by predation.
items.answer: Dark (melanic) moths increased in polluted areas in the 19th century and decreased after clean-air laws. Camouflage against the background affected predation by birds, changing allele frequencies.
items.markingKey: Context (Dark (melanic) moths increased in polluted areas in the 19th century and decreased after clean-air laws.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Camouflage against the background affected predation by birds, changing allele frequencies. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to natural selection by predation.

items.stem: After a drought, finches with larger beaks survived better. In the next generation, mean beak size increased. Why?
options: Beak size is heritable, so survivors passed on alleles for large beaks.
items.answer: Beak size is heritable, so survivors passed on alleles for large beaks.
items.markingKey: C. Heritable variation.

items.stem: In a population of beetles, the proportion of dark individuals rose from 12 % to 30 % over 10 generations. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Dark beetles had greater survival and reproduction under a selection pressure.
Beetles changed colour to match the background.
items.answer: Dark beetles had greater survival and reproduction under a selection pressure.
items.markingKey: B. Natural selection.

items.stem: Explain the process of natural selection and discuss evidence that it occurs, using named examples.
items.answer: Variation (mutation, meiosis, sexual reproduction); overproduction; competition; selection pressures (abiotic and biotic); differential survival and reproduction; inheritance; change in allele frequencies; examples: Galápagos finches, peppered moths, Endler’s guppies, antibiotic resistance.
items.markingKey: Variation (mutation, meiosis, sexual reproduction); overproduction; competition; selection pressures (abiotic and biotic); differential survival and reproduction; inheritance; change in allele frequencies; examples: Galápagos finches, peppered moths, Endler’s guppies, antibiotic resistance.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "stabilising selection".
items.answer: Selection that favours intermediate phenotypes and acts against both extremes
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: selection that favours intermediate phenotypes and acts against both extremes. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between directional selection and stabilising selection.
items.answer: Stabilising selection favours the intermediate phenotype and reduces variation without changing the mean; directional selection favours one extreme and shifts the mean.
items.markingKey: Stabilising selection favours the intermediate phenotype and reduces variation without changing the mean; directional selection favours one extreme and shifts the mean. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why do allele frequencies change if a population is not in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium?
options: Selection, mutation, migration, drift or non-random mating alter the gene pool.
items.answer: Selection, mutation, migration, drift or non-random mating alter the gene pool.
items.markingKey: D. Departures from conditions.

items.stem: Briefly describe African seedcracker finches and explain what it reveals about disruptive selection.
items.answer: Birds with either small or large beaks are common, but intermediate beaks are rare, matching two seed sizes. Intermediate beaks are inefficient for both seed types, so both extremes are favoured.
items.markingKey: Context (Birds with either small or large beaks are common, but intermediate beaks are rare, matching two seed sizes.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Intermediate beaks are inefficient for both seed types, so both extremes are favoured. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to disruptive selection.

items.stem:
The MN blood group is controlled by two codominant alleles, Lᴹ and Lᴺ. Blood samples from 899 people in a town were tested.

Blood group | Genotype | Number of people
M | LᴹLᴹ | 292
MN | LᴹLᴺ | 423
N | LᴺLᴺ | 184

(a) State the number of people with blood group MN. [1]
(b) Calculate the frequency of the Lᴹ allele. [2]
(c) Calculate the expected numbers of each genotype if the population is in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. [2]
Describe stabilising, directional and disruptive selection, using examples, and explain their effects on the distribution of phenotypes.
items.answer: Graphs; stabilising (birth mass) narrows distribution; directional (antibiotic resistance, finch beaks) shifts mean; disruptive (seedcracker finches) bimodal, possible speciation.
items.markingKey: Graphs; stabilising (birth mass) narrows distribution; directional (antibiotic resistance, finch beaks) shifts mean; disruptive (seedcracker finches) bimodal, possible speciation.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Selection that favours intermediate phenotypes and acts against both extremes"?
items.answer: stabilising selection
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of stabilising selection.

items.stem: A student claims: "Dominant alleles always increase in frequency over time." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Dominance does not affect frequency; without selection, frequencies stay constant (Hardy–Weinberg).
items.markingKey: Dominance does not affect frequency; without selection, frequencies stay constant (Hardy–Weinberg). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the three patterns of natural selection.
items.answer: Stabilising selection favours intermediate phenotypes, reducing variation (e.g. birth mass); directional selection favours one extreme, shifting the mean (e.g. antibiotic resistance); disruptive selection favours both extremes, possibly leading to two forms (e.g. beak sizes when seeds are small or large).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Stabilising selection favours intermediate phenotypes, reducing variation (e.g. birth mass); directional selection favours one extreme, shifting the mean (e.g. antibiotic resistance); disruptive selection favours both extremes, possibly leading to two forms (e.g. beak sizes when seeds are small or large). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The frequency of homozygous recessive individuals in a population is 0.01. Assuming Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, what is the frequency of heterozygotes?
Cystic fibrosis affects 1 in 2500 people of European descent. What is the approximate carrier frequency?
items.answer: 1 in 25

items.stem: "The Hardy–Weinberg principle is of little use because no real population meets its conditions." Discuss.
items.answer: Although no population meets the conditions exactly, the principle is very useful as a baseline for detecting evolution and estimating allele frequencies.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: real populations experience selection, migration and non-random mating. Arguments against: it provides a null model; deviations show evolution is occurring; it allows carrier frequencies to be estimated for genetic counselling. Supported judgement: Although no population meets the conditions exactly, the principle is very useful as a baseline for detecting evolution and estimating allele frequencies. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "maximum sustainable yield"?
options: The proportion of all copies of a gene in a population that are a particular allele
A critical threshold beyond which a small change causes a large, often irreversible, shift in an ecosystem
The warming of the Earth’s surface and lower atmosphere because greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit long-wave (infrared) radiation
The largest catch that can be taken from a population each year without reducing its size in the long term
items.answer: The largest catch that can be taken from a population each year without reducing its size in the long term
items.markingKey: D. "maximum sustainable yield" is the largest catch that can be taken from a population each year without reducing its size in the long term.

items.stem: Why does a persistent pesticide reach high concentrations in top predators?
options: It is not broken down or excreted and accumulates as predators eat many contaminated prey.
items.answer: It is not broken down or excreted and accumulates as predators eat many contaminated prey.
items.markingKey: C. Biomagnification.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain how eutrophication affects aquatic ecosystems.
items.answer: Nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers and sewage stimulate algal growth (bloom); algae block light, so submerged plants die; algae and plants die and are decomposed by aerobic bacteria; biochemical oxygen demand rises; oxygen falls; fish and invertebrates die; biodiversity decreases. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers and sewage stimulate algal growth (bloom); algae block light, so submerged plants die; algae and plants die and are decomposed by aerobic bacteria; biochemical oxygen demand rises; oxygen falls; fish and invertebrates die; biodiversity decreases. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe collapse of the Grand Banks cod fishery and explain what it reveals about tipping points and sustainability.
items.answer: Overfishing led to a moratorium in 1992; cod populations remained low for decades. Removing too many breeding fish pushed the ecosystem into a new state dominated by other species.
items.markingKey: Context (Overfishing led to a moratorium in 1992; cod populations remained low for decades.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Removing too many breeding fish pushed the ecosystem into a new state dominated by other species. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to tipping points and sustainability.

items.stem: "Adding nutrients to a lake always increases its biodiversity." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Excess nutrients cause eutrophication, oxygen depletion and loss of biodiversity.
items.markingKey: Excess nutrients cause eutrophication, oxygen depletion and loss of biodiversity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
A river was sampled at intervals downstream of a point where run-off from fertilised farmland and a sewage outlet enter it (0 m is just upstream of the outlet).

Distance / m | Dissolved O₂ / mg dm⁻³ | Nitrate / mg dm⁻³ | Number of invertebrate taxa
0 | 9.4 | 1.5 | 10
100 | 3.0 | 14.4 | 3
200 | 2.3 | 11.7 | 2
400 | 4.8 | 8.6 | 5
800 | 7.1 | 4.0 | 10
1600 | 8.8 | 2.2 | 13

(a) State the distance at which dissolved oxygen was lowest. [1]
(b) Calculate the percentage decrease in dissolved oxygen from 0 m to its lowest value. [2]
(c) Describe the relationship between nitrate concentration and the number of invertebrate taxa. [2]
items.answer: (a) 200 m (b) -75.5 % (c) Negative: where nitrate is highest, fewest taxa are found; taxa recover as nitrate decreases downstream.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 200 m (A1). (b) [2] (2.3 − 9.4)/9.4 × 100 (M1) = -75.5 % (A1). (c) [2] Negative relationship (A1); recovery downstream (A1).

items.stem: What is the main source of nitrates causing eutrophication?
items.answer: run-off of agricultural fertilisers
items.markingKey: B. Also sewage.

items.stem: Distinguish between unstable ecosystems and stable ecosystems.
items.answer: Stable ecosystems resist change and recover quickly after disturbance, typically with high biodiversity and complex food webs; unstable ecosystems change easily and may shift to a different state.
items.markingKey: Stable ecosystems resist change and recover quickly after disturbance, typically with high biodiversity and complex food webs; unstable ecosystems change easily and may shift to a different state. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why does a sealed mesocosm need light but not added food?
options: Producers capture light energy and nutrients are recycled by decomposers.
items.answer: Producers capture light energy and nutrients are recycled by decomposers.
items.markingKey: D. Energy flows; matter recycles.

items.stem: The concentration of a persistent pesticide (ppm) in a food chain was: water 3.3 × 10⁻⁵, plankton 5.4 × 10⁻⁴, small fish 0.013, large fish 0.11, fish-eating birds 0.83. Calculate the biomagnification factor from plankton to fish-eating birds.
items.answer: about 1500 times

items.stem: Explain the factors that affect the stability of ecosystems and evaluate the risk of tipping points.
items.answer: Biodiversity, food web complexity, keystone species, nutrient cycling, energy input; resilience; positive feedback; tipping points: Amazon, coral reefs, cod; eutrophication; biomagnification; mesocosms; sustainable practices.
items.markingKey: Biodiversity, food web complexity, keystone species, nutrient cycling, energy input; resilience; positive feedback; tipping points: Amazon, coral reefs, cod; eutrophication; biomagnification; mesocosms; sustainable practices.

items.stem: "Ecosystems are resilient enough to recover from any human disturbance." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Ecosystems can be resilient, but beyond tipping points recovery may be impossible, so precautionary management is needed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: many systems recover after pollution is reduced, e.g. birds of prey after DDT bans, rivers after clean-up. Arguments against: tipping points such as cod collapse and coral reef shifts may be irreversible; combined stresses reduce resilience. Supported judgement: Ecosystems can be resilient, but beyond tipping points recovery may be impossible, so precautionary management is needed. Markbands (8 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which greenhouse gas is produced by cattle and rice paddies?
items.answer: methane
items.markingKey: methane. From anaerobic microbes.

items.stem: Why is methane a significant greenhouse gas despite its low concentration?
options: Each molecule absorbs much more infrared radiation than a CO₂ molecule.
items.answer: Each molecule absorbs much more infrared radiation than a CO₂ molecule.
items.markingKey: B. Global warming potential.

items.stem: Explain how positive feedback mechanisms can accelerate climate change.
items.answer: Melting ice reduces albedo, so more heat is absorbed; thawing permafrost releases CO₂ and methane; warmer oceans absorb less CO₂; drought and fires release carbon from forests; each process causes further warming, possibly crossing tipping points.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Melting ice reduces albedo, so more heat is absorbed; thawing permafrost releases CO₂ and methane; warmer oceans absorb less CO₂; drought and fires release carbon from forests; each process causes further warming, possibly crossing tipping points. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Alessia writes: "Climate change only affects temperature." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It also changes rainfall, sea level, ocean pH, extreme weather and the timing of biological events.
items.markingKey: It also changes rainfall, sea level, ocean pH, extreme weather and the timing of biological events. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The breeding population of an Arctic seabird changed from 6006 pairs to 3779 pairs over 30 years as sea ice declined. Calculate the percentage change and suggest a biological explanation for it.
items.answer: -37.1 %; loss of sea ice reduced the populations of ice-associated prey such as Arctic cod, so less food was available.
items.markingKey: % change = (3779 − 6006)/6006 × 100 (M1) = -37.1 % (A1). Explanation (R1): loss of sea ice reduced the populations of ice-associated prey such as Arctic cod, so less food was available.

items.stem: Explain the causes of anthropogenic climate change and its effects on ecosystems.
items.answer: Greenhouse effect; CO₂ from fossil fuels and deforestation; methane from agriculture; Keeling curve; positive feedback (albedo, permafrost); effects: range shifts, phenology mismatch, coral bleaching, ocean acidification, polar habitats, extinction risk; mitigation and adaptation.
items.markingKey: Greenhouse effect; CO₂ from fossil fuels and deforestation; methane from agriculture; Keeling curve; positive feedback (albedo, permafrost); effects: range shifts, phenology mismatch, coral bleaching, ocean acidification, polar habitats, extinction risk; mitigation and adaptation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "range shift"?
options: A change in the geographical distribution of a species, e.g. towards the poles or higher altitudes as the climate warms
All the alleles of all the genes in a population at a given time
The timing of seasonal biological events such as flowering, leaf opening, migration and breeding
An environmental factor, such as predation, disease or competition, that affects the survival and reproduction of individuals with particular traits
items.answer: A change in the geographical distribution of a species, e.g. towards the poles or higher altitudes as the climate warms
items.markingKey: A. "range shift" is a change in the geographical distribution of a species, e.g. towards the poles or higher altitudes as the climate warms.

items.stem: Explain the difference between mitigation and adaptation.
items.answer: Mitigation reduces the causes of climate change (cutting emissions, increasing sinks); adaptation reduces its impacts (sea walls, drought-resistant crops, conservation corridors).
items.markingKey: Mitigation reduces the causes of climate change (cutting emissions, increasing sinks); adaptation reduces its impacts (sea walls, drought-resistant crops, conservation corridors). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: An Arctic species is restricted to tundra. Why is it particularly threatened by warming?
options: Its habitat shrinks as the treeline moves north, and it has nowhere colder to move to.
It can move to the equator.
items.answer: Its habitat shrinks as the treeline moves north, and it has nowhere colder to move to.
items.markingKey: B. Habitat loss.

items.stem: Using great tits and winter moth caterpillars in Wytham Woods as an example, explain phenological mismatch.
items.answer: Oak leaves and caterpillars emerge earlier with warming, but great tits have advanced egg-laying less. Chicks hatch after the caterpillar peak, reducing food and breeding success.
items.markingKey: Context (Oak leaves and caterpillars emerge earlier with warming, but great tits have advanced egg-laying less.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Chicks hatch after the caterpillar peak, reducing food and breeding success. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to phenological mismatch.

items.stem: "Ecosystems will be able to adapt to climate change without human help." Discuss.
items.answer: Some species will adapt, but the speed of change and habitat fragmentation mean many will not without conservation measures and emission cuts.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: species have shifted ranges and phenology in response to past climate changes; some populations show rapid evolutionary change. Arguments against: current change is much faster than past natural change; habitat fragmentation blocks movement; tipping points such as coral loss. Supported judgement: Some species will adapt, but the speed of change and habitat fragmentation mean many will not without conservation measures and emission cuts. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which is a source of heritable variation?
items.answer: mutation
items.markingKey: C. New alleles.

items.stem: Which is an example of stabilising selection?
options: human birth mass, where very low and very high masses have higher mortality
items.answer: human birth mass, where very low and very high masses have higher mortality
items.markingKey: B. Intermediate favoured.

items.stem: What causes the oxygen depletion in eutrophication?
items.answer: aerobic decomposition of dead algae by bacteria
items.markingKey: aerobic decomposition of dead algae by bacteria. Increased BOD.

items.stem: Why does ocean acidification harm shelled organisms?
options: Lower pH reduces carbonate ion availability, making it harder to build calcium carbonate shells.
items.answer: Lower pH reduces carbonate ion availability, making it harder to build calcium carbonate shells.
items.markingKey: C. Carbonate chemistry.

items.stem: Explain how sexual selection can lead to traits that reduce survival.
items.answer: Traits such as bright colours or long tails increase mating success through female choice or male competition; individuals with them produce more offspring even if they are more vulnerable to predators; the trait spreads if reproductive benefit exceeds survival cost.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Traits such as bright colours or long tails increase mating success through female choice or male competition; individuals with them produce more offspring even if they are more vulnerable to predators; the trait spreads if reproductive benefit exceeds survival cost. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between natural selection and artificial selection.
items.answer: In natural selection the environment determines which individuals reproduce; in artificial selection humans choose individuals with desired traits to breed.
items.markingKey: In natural selection the environment determines which individuals reproduce; in artificial selection humans choose individuals with desired traits to breed. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between bioaccumulation and biomagnification.
items.answer: Bioaccumulation is the build-up of a pollutant within an individual organism over time; biomagnification is the increase in concentration from one trophic level to the next.
items.markingKey: Bioaccumulation is the build-up of a pollutant within an individual organism over time; biomagnification is the increase in concentration from one trophic level to the next. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the enhanced greenhouse effect.
items.answer: Short-wave radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface; the surface emits long-wave infrared; greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, H₂O) absorb and re-emit it, warming the atmosphere; human activities (fossil fuel combustion, deforestation, agriculture) increase greenhouse gas concentrations, so more heat is retained.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Short-wave radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface; the surface emits long-wave infrared; greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, H₂O) absorb and re-emit it, warming the atmosphere; human activities (fossil fuel combustion, deforestation, agriculture) increase greenhouse gas concentrations, so more heat is retained. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between acquired characteristics and heritable variation.
items.answer: Heritable variation is genetic and passed to offspring; acquired characteristics develop during life (e.g. muscles, scars) and are not inherited.
items.markingKey: Heritable variation is genetic and passed to offspring; acquired characteristics develop during life (e.g. muscles, scars) and are not inherited. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of individuals showing red–green colour blindness (in a hypothetical autosomal model) (homozygous recessive) is 0.0128. Calculate the frequency of the recessive allele, the dominant allele and of heterozygous carriers.
Buffer strips of vegetation between fields and rivers help to:
options: absorb nutrients from run-off and reduce eutrophication
items.answer: absorb nutrients from run-off and reduce eutrophication
items.markingKey: C. Sustainable farming.

items.stem: The frequency of the dominant allele is 0.4. What proportion of the population shows the dominant phenotype?
After nitrate fertiliser run-off, a lake’s dissolved oxygen fell sharply. Which sequence explains this?
options: fish increase → oxygen used → algae die
algal bloom → algae die → bacterial decomposition uses oxygen
items.answer: algal bloom → algae die → bacterial decomposition uses oxygen
items.markingKey: C. Eutrophication.

items.stem: A butterfly’s northern range edge has moved 100 km north in 30 years. What is the mean rate?
items.answer: about 3.3 km per year

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Natural selection is the only mechanism of evolutionary change."
items.answer: Natural selection is the main cause of adaptation, but other mechanisms such as drift also change allele frequencies.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains adaptation in many examples (finches, moths, antibiotic resistance). Arguments against: genetic drift and gene flow change allele frequencies randomly or by migration; mutation supplies variation; sexual selection is a distinct process. Supported judgement: Natural selection is the main cause of adaptation, but other mechanisms such as drift also change allele frequencies.

items.stem: Explain the Hardy–Weinberg principle, the conditions under which it applies and how it can be used to study evolution.
items.answer: Gene pool; p + q = 1; p² + 2pq + q² = 1; conditions; calculation of carrier frequency; testing equilibrium with chi-squared; departures show selection, drift, migration, mutation; examples sickle-cell, CF.
items.markingKey: Gene pool; p + q = 1; p² + 2pq + q² = 1; conditions; calculation of carrier frequency; testing equilibrium with chi-squared; departures show selection, drift, migration, mutation; examples sickle-cell, CF.

items.stem:
A river was sampled at intervals downstream of a point where run-off from fertilised farmland and a sewage outlet enter it (0 m is just upstream of the outlet).

Distance / m | Dissolved O₂ / mg dm⁻³ | Nitrate / mg dm⁻³ | Number of invertebrate taxa
0 | 9.0 | 1.5 | 11
100 | 3.0 | 13.8 | 3
200 | 2.1 | 12.8 | 2
400 | 4.4 | 8.0 | 5
800 | 7.0 | 4.3 | 10
1600 | 8.9 | 1.9 | 12

(a) State the distance at which dissolved oxygen was lowest. [1]
(b) Calculate the percentage decrease in dissolved oxygen from 0 m to its lowest value. [2]
(c) Describe the relationship between nitrate concentration and the number of invertebrate taxa. [2]
(d) Explain why dissolved oxygen falls downstream of the outlet. [3]
items.answer: (a) 200 m (b) -76.7 % (c) Negative: where nitrate is highest, fewest taxa are found; taxa recover as nitrate decreases downstream. (d) Nutrients cause algal growth; dead algae and organic sewage are decomposed by aerobic bacteria; high biochemical oxygen demand uses up oxygen.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 200 m (A1). (b) [2] (2.1 − 9.0)/9.0 × 100 (M1) = -76.7 % (A1). (c) [2] Negative relationship (A1); recovery downstream (A1). (d) [3] Nutrients/algae (A1); decomposition (A1); BOD (A1).

items.stem: "Ecosystems will be able to adapt to climate change without human help." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Some species will adapt, but the speed of change and habitat fragmentation mean many will not without conservation measures and emission cuts.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: species have shifted ranges and phenology in response to past climate changes; some populations show rapid evolutionary change. Arguments against: current change is much faster than past natural change; habitat fragmentation blocks movement; tipping points such as coral loss. Supported judgement: Some species will adapt, but the speed of change and habitat fragmentation mean many will not without conservation measures and emission cuts. Markbands (8 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "selection pressure"?
options: The proportion of all copies of a gene in a population that are a particular allele
An environmental factor, such as predation, disease or competition, that affects the survival and reproduction of individuals with particular traits
The principle that allele and genotype frequencies remain constant between generations if there is no selection, mutation, migration or genetic drift and mating is random: p² + 2pq + q² = 1
The selective breeding of organisms by humans for desired characteristics
items.answer: An environmental factor, such as predation, disease or competition, that affects the survival and reproduction of individuals with particular traits
items.markingKey: B. "selection pressure" is an environmental factor, such as predation, disease or competition, that affects the survival and reproduction of individuals with particular traits.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "gene pool"?
options: All the alleles of all the genes in a population at a given time
A critical threshold beyond which a small change causes a large, often irreversible, shift in an ecosystem
The ability of an ecosystem to recover after a disturbance
The timing of seasonal biological events such as flowering, leaf opening, migration and breeding
items.answer: All the alleles of all the genes in a population at a given time
items.markingKey: A. "gene pool" is all the alleles of all the genes in a population at a given time.

items.stem: Define the term "maximum sustainable yield".
items.answer: The largest catch that can be taken from a population each year without reducing its size in the long term
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the largest catch that can be taken from a population each year without reducing its size in the long term. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Why do many species shift their ranges towards the poles?
options: Warming makes formerly cold areas suitable and lowers survival in warmer parts of their range.
items.answer: Warming makes formerly cold areas suitable and lowers survival in warmer parts of their range.
items.markingKey: A. Track suitable climate.

items.stem: Tariq writes: "Individual organisms evolve during their lifetime." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Populations evolve over generations as allele frequencies change; individuals do not.
items.markingKey: Populations evolve over generations as allele frequencies change; individuals do not. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Dominant alleles always increase in frequency over time." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Dominance does not affect frequency; without selection, frequencies stay constant (Hardy–Weinberg).
items.markingKey: Dominance does not affect frequency; without selection, frequencies stay constant (Hardy–Weinberg). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "Adding nutrients to a lake always increases its biodiversity." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Excess nutrients cause eutrophication, oxygen depletion and loss of biodiversity.
items.markingKey: Excess nutrients cause eutrophication, oxygen depletion and loss of biodiversity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "The greenhouse effect is caused by the hole in the ozone layer." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Ozone depletion increases UV reaching the surface; the greenhouse effect is due to gases absorbing infrared.
items.markingKey: Ozone depletion increases UV reaching the surface; the greenhouse effect is due to gases absorbing infrared. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why are bright colours in male guppies less common in streams with many predators?
options: Brightly coloured males are more visible and more likely to be eaten.
items.answer: Brightly coloured males are more visible and more likely to be eaten.
items.markingKey: C. Natural selection opposes sexual selection.

items.stem: In a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of individuals showing albinism (homozygous recessive) is 0.0046. Calculate the frequency of the recessive allele, the dominant allele and of heterozygous carriers.
Cod in the Grand Banks collapsed in 1992 and have not fully recovered. What does this suggest?
options: Cod recover immediately once fishing stops.
A tipping point was crossed and the ecosystem shifted to a new stable state.
items.answer: A tipping point was crossed and the ecosystem shifted to a new stable state.
items.markingKey: D. Alternative stable states.

items.stem: Polar bear populations decline as sea ice shrinks. Why?
options: They hunt seals from sea ice, so less ice means less food.
items.answer: They hunt seals from sea ice, so less ice means less food.
items.markingKey: D. Habitat loss.

items.stem: The frequency of the melanic form of the peppered moth near Manchester changed from 90 % to 36 % after clean-air legislation. Calculate the percentage change and suggest a biological explanation for it.
items.answer: -60.0 %; cleaner tree bark made dark moths more visible to bird predators, so pale moths had a survival advantage.
items.markingKey: % change = (36 − 90)/90 × 100 (M1) = -60.0 % (A1). Explanation (R1): cleaner tree bark made dark moths more visible to bird predators, so pale moths had a survival advantage.

items.answer: about 2600 times

items.stem:
The MN blood group is controlled by two codominant alleles, Lᴹ and Lᴺ. Blood samples from 913 people in a town were tested.

Blood group | Genotype | Number of people
M | LᴹLᴹ | 133
MN | LᴹLᴺ | 436
N | LᴺLᴺ | 344

(a) State the number of people with blood group MN. [1]
(b) Calculate the frequency of the Lᴹ allele. [2]
(c) Calculate the expected numbers of each genotype if the population is in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. [2]

items.answer: (a) 436 (b) p = 0.384 (c) M 134.9; MN 432.1; N 345.9 (d) χ² = 0.07; no significant deviation – consistent with equilibrium

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Ecosystems are resilient enough to recover from any human disturbance."
items.answer: Ecosystems can be resilient, but beyond tipping points recovery may be impossible, so precautionary management is needed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: many systems recover after pollution is reduced, e.g. birds of prey after DDT bans, rivers after clean-up. Arguments against: tipping points such as cod collapse and coral reef shifts may be irreversible; combined stresses reduce resilience. Supported judgement: Ecosystems can be resilient, but beyond tipping points recovery may be impossible, so precautionary management is needed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.
